title: Growing runner beans
subtitle: Supporting, watering, and picking a runner bean wigwam through summer
excerpt: Runner beans are planted outdoors after the last frost in May and climbed up canes or a wigwam through summer. They need regular picking to keep producing and plenty of water once the flowers open. A well-managed wigwam crops for two to three months.
sourceNotes: Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), kitchen garden section. RHS runner bean growing guide (rhs.org.uk). USDA agricultural extension notes on climbing bean production, public domain.

glossaryTerms.definition: A trench dug the previous autumn and filled over winter with kitchen waste, grass cuttings, and cardboard before covering with soil in spring. Runner beans planted over the filled trench have a moisture-retaining, nutrient-rich root run that sustains a heavy cropping season. The traditional UK allotment preparation method for runner beans.

content.text: Runner beans are a UK allotment classic: frost-tender climbing plants grown up canes or a wigwam, harvested from July through to October. The key to a long harvest is picking the pods before the seeds inside swell; beans left to ripen on the plant stop producing new flowers. Plant outdoors after the last frost, water heavily once in flower, and pick every two to three days at peak season.
Full sun, sheltered from wind. Rich, moisture-retentive soil. Runner beans are heavy feeders and heavy drinkers; a
prepared the previous autumn gives excellent results. If you haven't prepared a trench, work plenty of well-rotted compost into the bed before planting.

Sow indoors in late April, one seed per 9 cm pot, 5 cm deep. Plant out in late May after the last frost. Alternatively, sow direct outdoors from late May. Spacing: 15 cm between plants in double rows 60 cm apart, or around a wigwam of 8 to 10 canes (2.4 m tall) with one plant per cane. Put the support structure in first, then plant.

Water deeply once a week in dry weather. From flowering onwards, increase to two to three times a week; water stress at flowering causes the blooms to drop without setting a pod. A mulch of 8 to 10 cm of compost around the base retains moisture and feeds the roots. Train the leading shoots onto the canes as they grow; the plants begin twining naturally but the first 20 cm needs guiding.

Pick when the pods are 15 to 20 cm long and still flat; once you can feel the seeds swelling inside the pod, the bean is past its best and the plant slows production. Check the plants every two days during the July and August peak. Pick even if you can't use the beans immediately; leaving them on the plant stops the plant producing new ones. Pick at the end of October before the first hard frost and compost the roots.

items.cause: Drought, high temperatures, or lack of pollinators.
items.fix: Water heavily from flowering onwards. Plant borage or phacelia nearby to attract bees. Shade with fleece during heatwaves above 30°C.

items.symptom: Black fly clustering on new growing tips
items.fix: Pinch out affected tips. Spray with a jet of water. Encourage ladybirds and hoverflies by planting umbellifers nearby.

items.symptom: Pods become tough and stringy before they look large enough to pick
items.cause: Old or slower-maturing variety, or warm weather hastening maturity.
items.fix: Grow stringless varieties such as Enorma, Polestar, or Lady Di. Pick earlier, testing from 12 to 15 cm.
